notes.summary: A time series is a set of values recorded at successive points of time, such as yearly sales or monthly prices. Paper 2 asks you to name the four components (trend, seasonal, cyclical, irregular), choose between the additive and multiplicative models, measure trend by the graphic, semi-average, moving-average and least-squares methods, and work with seasonal indices.

concepts.title: What a time series is
concepts.body:
• Data arranged in order of time: Y1, Y2, … at times t1, t2, …
  • Uses: understanding past behaviour, forecasting, comparing series, and planning (production, stock, budgets).
  • Analysis means separating the series into its components so each can be studied on its own.

concepts.title: The four components
concepts.body:
ComponentWhat it isExample
Secular trend (T)Long-term smooth rise or fall over many yearsGrowth of population, steady rise in prices
Seasonal variation (S)Regular pattern that repeats within a year (period up to one year)More woollens sold in winter, more ice-cream in summer, bank rush at month end
Cyclical variation (C)Up-and-down waves lasting more than a year, not of fixed lengthBusiness cycle: prosperity, recession, depression, recovery
Irregular variation (I)Random, unpredictable, short-lived changesFloods, earthquakes, wars, strikes, pandemics

Seasonal and cyclical variations are both periodic (they repeat); irregular variations are not.

concepts.title: Additive and multiplicative models
concepts.body:
AdditiveMultiplicative
ModelY = T + S + C + IY = T × S × C × I
AssumesComponents are independent of each otherComponents affect each other (seasonal swing grows with the trend)
S, C, I measured asAbsolute amounts in the same units as YRatios or percentages (indices) around 1 or 100
Seasonal effects add to0 over a year400% for quarters, 1200% for months

The multiplicative model is used more often in practice. Taking logarithms turns it into an additive model: log Y = log T + log S + log C + log I.

Example: T = 200, S = 110%, C = 95%, I = 100%. Multiplicative Y = 200 × 1.10 × 0.95 × 1 = 209.

concepts.title: Methods of measuring trend
concepts.body:
MethodHowStrengthWeakness
Free-hand (graphic)Plot the data and draw a smooth line by eyeSimplest, quickSubjective: different people draw different lines
Semi-averagesAverage each half and join the two pointsObjective, easyAssumes a straight line; affected by extreme values
Moving averagesAverage successive groups of k valuesSmooths out regular cycles of length k; flexibleLoses values at both ends; no equation for forecasting
Least squaresFit y = a + bx by minimising Σ(y − ŷ)²Objective, gives an equation for forecastingMore calculation; the curve type must be chosen in advance

concepts.title: Method of semi-averages
concepts.body:
• Split the data into two equal halves. If the number of years is odd, leave out the middle year.
  • Find the average of each half and place it at the middle of that half.
  • Join the two points. Slope per year = (difference of the averages) ÷ (gap in years between the two centres).

Example: 2017–2022: 20, 24, 22, 28, 30, 32. First half average = 22 (at 2018); second half average = 30 (at 2021). Slope = 8/3 ≈ 2.67 per year.

concepts.title: Method of moving averages
concepts.body:
• Odd period (3, 5, …): average each group of k values and place it against the middle year.
  • Even period (4, 6, …): the averages fall between two years, so take a 2-item moving average of them to centre them.
  • The period should equal the length of the cycle in the data; then the cycle is removed completely.
  • A k-period moving average loses (k − 1)/2 values at each end for odd k.

concepts.title: Method of least squares
concepts.body:
• Straight-line trend y = a + bx. Normal equations: Σy = na + bΣx and Σxy = aΣx + bΣx².
  • Choose the origin at the middle so that Σx = 0. Then a = Σy/n and b = Σxy/Σx².
  • Odd n: x = year − middle year (…, −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, …).
  • Even n: origin between the two middle years and x = 2 × (year − origin), giving …, −3, −1, 1, 3, …; then b is the change per half-year.
  • a is the trend value at the origin; b is the change per unit of x.
  • The sum of deviations Σ(y − ŷ) = 0 and Σ(y − ŷ)² is the least possible.
  • Other curves: parabola y = a + bx + cx², exponential y = abx (fit log y = log a + x log b).
  • Annual trend y = a + bx (x in years, y annual totals) becomes a monthly trend y = a/12 + (b/144)x with x in months.

Example: 2018–2022 values 12, 15, 14, 18, 21, origin 2020. Σy = 80, a = 16. Σxy = −24 − 15 + 0 + 18 + 42 = 21, Σx² = 10, b = 2.1. Trend: y = 16 + 2.1x. For 2024 (x = 4): 24.4.

concepts.title: Seasonal indices
concepts.body:
• A seasonal index shows each season's typical level as a percentage of the average season. Average index = 100.
  • Quarterly indices add to 400; monthly indices add to 1200. If they do not, multiply each by 400/sum (or 1200/sum).
  • Method of simple averages: average each quarter over the years, then index = quarter average ÷ grand average × 100.
  • Ratio to trend: divide each value by its trend value (from least squares), then average the ratios for each season.
  • Ratio to moving average: divide each value by the centred 4-quarter (or 12-month) moving average; the most widely used method.
  • Link relatives: each season as a percentage of the previous season, chained together.
  • Deseasonalised value = actual value ÷ seasonal index × 100.

Example: quarter averages 30, 40, 50, 40; grand average 40. Indices: 75, 100, 125, 100 (sum 400). Actual Q3 sales of 150 deseasonalise to 150 ÷ 1.25 = 120.

varieties.name: Components of a time series
varieties.how: Within a year and regular is seasonal; waves of more than a year are cyclical; long-term direction is trend; sudden, one-off events are irregular.

example.q: Sales of a company fall sharply for one month because of a flood. This is an example of:
steps: A flood is sudden, unpredictable and does not repeat on a schedule.

varieties.name: Additive and multiplicative models
varieties.how: Additive: Y = T + S + C + I with components in units. Multiplicative: Y = T × S × C × I with S, C, I as ratios (divide indices by 100).

example.q: Under the multiplicative model, the trend value is 200, the seasonal index is 110, the cyclical index is 95 and the irregular index is 100. Find the expected value.

varieties.name: Method of semi-averages
varieties.how: Average each half (drop the middle year if the count is odd), place each average at its half's middle year, and join them.

example.q: Values for 2017–2022 are 20, 24, 22, 28, 30, 32. Using semi-averages, find the trend value for 2023.

varieties.name: Moving averages
varieties.how: Odd period: average the group and place it at the middle. Even period: average consecutive moving averages in pairs to centre them.

example.q: Values for 6 years are 10, 12, 14, 18, 20, 22. Find the 4-year centred moving average for year 3.
steps: 4-year averages: 13.5 and 16, which sit between years 2–3 and 3–4.

varieties.name: Least-squares trend line
varieties.how: Put the origin at the middle so Σx = 0. Then a = Σy/n, b = Σxy/Σx², and trend = a + bx.

example.q: Values for 2018–2022 are 12, 15, 14, 18, 21. Fit a straight-line trend (origin 2020) and estimate 2024.

varieties.name: Seasonal indices
varieties.how: Index = season average ÷ grand average × 100. Quarterly indices total 400 (monthly 1200). Deseasonalised value = actual ÷ index × 100.

example.q: Quarterly averages over several years are 30, 40, 50 and 40. Find the seasonal index for Q3, and the deseasonalised value of Q3 sales of 150.

tips: "Every year", "every winter", "festival season" point to seasonal variation.
For least squares, always shift the origin to the middle so Σx = 0; it makes a and b one-line divisions.
With an even number of years, use x = −5, −3, −1, 1, 3, 5 (half-year units) and remember b is per half-year.
If seasonal indices do not total 400 (or 1200), scale each by 400/total.
The period of a moving average should match the length of the cycle in the data.
traps: Seasonal variation is within a year; cyclical variation lasts more than a year.
Even-period moving averages must be centred before placing them against a year.
In the multiplicative model, convert indices to ratios (110 → 1.10) before multiplying.
Moving averages give no trend values for the first and last few years.
In the semi-average method with an odd number of years, the middle year is left out.

formulas.name: Normal equations
formulas.expr: Σy = na + bΣx;  Σxy = aΣx + bΣx²

formulas.name: Semi-average slope
formulas.expr: b = (second average − first average) ÷ years between centres

questions.q: More woollen clothes are sold every winter. This variation is:
questions.solution: The pattern repeats every year within the year, so it is seasonal variation.

questions.q: Fluctuations caused by business cycles (boom, recession, depression, recovery) are called:
questions.solution: Business-cycle waves last more than a year and are called cyclical variations.

questions.q: Sales for 5 years are 10, 14, 18, 16, 20. The 3-year moving average centred on the 3rd year is:
A trend equation is y = 50 + 4x with origin 2020 and x in years. The trend value for 2025 is:
Values for 2019–2023 are 10, 12, 15, 17, 21. Fitting a straight-line trend by least squares (origin 2021), the estimate for 2025 is:
Seasonal indices for Q1, Q2 and Q3 are 90, 110 and 120. The index for Q4 is:
questions.solution:
Quarterly seasonal indices add up to 400.
Q4 = 400 − (90 + 110 + 120) = 400 − 320 = 80.
